title: Using tolerances to manage constraints
blurb: Describe how tolerances for the seven aspects are set at project, stage and work package level, and how delivery sustainability enters planning.
question: A team manager forecasts that a work package will finish later than its time tolerance allows. To whom should this be escalated, and why?

teach.body: Every project works within constraints such as a deadline, a budget or a required scope. PRINCE2 manages them with tolerances: the permissible deviation above and below a plan's target before the matter must be escalated to the next level of management. Tolerances can be set for benefits, time, cost, quality, scope, risk and sustainability at each level of plan. Plain English: 'aim for this, and you may drift this far before you must tell us'.

teach.caption: The same seven aspects of performance. Sustainability is new in PRINCE2 7; older material lists only six.

head: Tolerance
Permissible deviation in
rows: Finishing later or earlier than target
teach.caption: Quality tolerance is drawn from the prioritized acceptance criteria and the quality specifications in product descriptions.

teach.body: Understanding which constraints matter most is crucial to choosing the right approach and setting sensible tolerances. If a product must be ready for a fixed event, time tolerance may be close to zero while cost or scope tolerance is wider. If the budget is capped, cost tolerance is tight and something else must flex. Tolerances express those priorities in numbers.

teach.caption: Project tolerances are documented in the project mandate or confirmed to the board for the project brief. The executive defines tolerances for each stage.

teach.h: A breach is forecast: where does it go?
teach.caption: An exception is a forecast breach, not only an actual one. The project manager instructs corrective action when work package tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.

teach.h: Tolerances in a work package description
teach.note: Work package targets and tolerances cover scope, cost and time. Quality is controlled through the product descriptions instead.

teach.body: PRINCE2 7 treats sustainability as a performance target equal to time, cost and the rest. Its sustainability management approach covers the sustainability of the project work as well as the whole-life sustainability of the project product. When planning, the project manager therefore considers how the work itself is delivered, for example travel, materials and energy used, and how the team works, not just how sustainable the finished product will be.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Tamsley Council's flood barrier
teach.body: Tamsley Council must have a flood barrier working before winter. Its business layer sets a time tolerance of two weeks and a cost tolerance of 10%. The board gives the stage a one-week time tolerance and a carbon limit for site works. Project manager Dev Patel gives the steelwork package a scope, cost and time tolerance. When team manager Lucy Ward forecasts a four-day slip beyond it, she raises it with Dev, who resolves it within stage tolerance without involving the board.

teach.text: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits and quality tolerances are not agreed in a work package description. Also remember that an exception is a forecast breach: a team manager escalates to the project manager, never straight to the board, and only stage or project exceptions go to the board.

items: Seven tolerance areas: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability, risk (7.2.4).
Knowing which constraint takes precedence guides the approach and the tolerances set.
Business layer sets project tolerances; the board (executive) sets stage tolerances; the PM sets work package tolerances.
WPD tolerances: scope, cost and time only.
Delivery sustainability: plan for the sustainability of the project work, not only of the product.

summary: You can now explain how tolerances for the seven aspects manage a project's constraints, who sets them at project, stage and work package level, and where forecast breaches are escalated. You can also explain why delivery sustainability is considered when planning.

A.q: Which tolerance describes the permissible variation of a plan's products?
A.why: Scope tolerance is the permissible variation of the plan's products (7.2.4, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: Quality tolerance is variation from the agreed quality criteria.
whyNot.1: Benefits tolerance is under- or over-delivery of benefits.
whyNot.2: Risk tolerance limits the plan's aggregated risks.

A.q: Who sets the tolerances for each stage?
A.why: The project board sets stage tolerances; the executive defines the tolerances for each stage and approves stage plans (tab 7.1, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: The business layer sets project tolerances.
whyNot.1: The project manager sets work package tolerances.
whyNot.3: Project assurance reviews progress against agreed tolerances; it does not set them.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. PRINCE2 7 sets tolerances for benefits, time, cost, quality, scope, risk and [?].
A.why: PRINCE2 7 added sustainability as the seventh aspect with its own tolerance (7.2.4).

whyNot.0: Resources are planned, but resources are not one of the seven tolerance areas.
whyNot.2: Stakeholders are managed through the people element and communication approach, not a tolerance.
whyNot.3: Communication is handled by the communication management approach, not a tolerance.

B.q:
Which two statements about tolerances in a work package description are correct?
1. They include time tolerance.
2. They include benefits tolerance.
3. They include cost tolerance.
4. They include quality tolerance.
B.why: A work package description sets targets and tolerances for scope, cost and time; benefits and quality tolerances are not in a WPD (7.5, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: benefits tolerance is not agreed at work package level.
whyNot.2: Both are false: benefits and quality tolerances are not set in a WPD.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: quality is controlled through product descriptions, not WPD tolerance.

B.q: A team manager forecasts that a work package will exceed its time tolerance. What should happen?
options: The team manager raises it with the project manager as an issue
The team manager sends an exception report to the project board
The team manager asks the business layer for more time
The team manager extends the work package and records it later
B.why: Team managers escalate forecast work package breaches to the project manager as an issue; the PM handles work-package-level exceptions in controlling a stage (11.2.1, 11.2.6).

whyNot.1: Exception reports go from the project manager to the board, for stage or project tolerance.
whyNot.2: The business layer deals with project-level exceptions, and a team manager reports to the project manager.
whyNot.3: Working outside agreed tolerance without escalating defeats manage by exception.

B.q: Why is it important to understand which constraints take precedence when planning?
options: It decides which stage plans need an exception plan
It shows which risks go into the risk register
It guides the approach chosen and the tolerances set
It fixes how many work packages the stage contains
B.why: Knowing which constraints take precedence is crucial to choosing approaches and setting tolerances (7.2.4).

whyNot.0: Exception plans follow exception reports when the board decides to address them.
whyNot.1: Risks are recorded in the register when identified, not according to constraint priority.
whyNot.3: Work packages are organized from the products and delivery approach, not from constraint priority.

C.q: Who sets the project tolerances, and where are they first documented?
options: The project board; in the project plan
The executive; in the business case
The project manager; in the project brief
The business layer; in the project mandate
C.why: The business layer sets project tolerances and documents them in the project mandate, or confirms them to the board for inclusion in the project brief (tab 7.1).

whyNot.0: The board sets stage tolerances and works within project tolerances set by the business layer.
whyNot.1: The executive defines stage tolerances; project tolerances come from the business layer.
whyNot.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances, not project tolerances.

C.q: A project manager forecasts that the current stage will exceed its cost tolerance. Which product should be raised, and who receives it?
options: An exception report; the project board
An issue report; the team manager
A highlight report; the business layer
C.why: A forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated by the project manager to the project board in an exception report (11.2.6, 11.3.1).

whyNot.1: Issue reports cover issues handled formally, and team managers do not decide stage tolerance breaches.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports give the board regular status; the business layer handles project-level, not stage-level, exceptions.
whyNot.3: Checkpoint reports go from team manager to project manager on work package status.

C.q: When planning, a project manager looks at the travel, materials and energy that the project work itself will use. Which consideration is this?
C.why: Delivery sustainability concerns the sustainability of how the project work is carried out, as distinct from the whole-life sustainability of the product (7.4.4).

whyNot.0: Benefits tolerance limits under- or over-delivery of benefits.
whyNot.2: Quality criteria describe what the product must meet, not how the work is delivered.
whyNot.3: Scope tolerance limits variation of the plan's products.

reteach.title: Nested allowances
reteach.question: A finance director gives a department a budget with a margin, the department head gives each team a slice with a smaller margin. How is that like PRINCE2 tolerances?

blocks.h: Each level stays inside the one above
blocks.body: The business layer gives the project its tolerances. The board passes a share to each stage. The project manager passes a share to each work package. As long as a level is forecast to stay inside its own allowance, it carries on; if it is forecast to go outside, it escalates to the level that set the allowance.

blocks.h: Tolerances flow down, exceptions flow up

blocks.text: The level that sets a tolerance is the level that receives the exception. A work package exception goes to the project manager, not the board.

explain.body: Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk can each have a tolerance at each level of plan.

test.q: Which tolerance limits the plan's aggregated risks?
test.why: Risk tolerance sets limits on the plan's aggregated risks (11.2.1).

whyNot.0: Scope tolerance covers variation of the plan's products.
whyNot.1: Quality tolerance covers variation from agreed quality criteria.
whyNot.3: Benefits tolerance covers under- or over-delivery of benefits.

explain.body: The project manager sets work package tolerances and instructs corrective action when they are forecast to be exceeded, within the stage tolerance.

test.q: Who instructs corrective action when work-package-level tolerances are forecast to be exceeded?
test.why: The project manager instructs corrective action when work-package-level tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (tab 7.1).

whyNot.0: The executive defines stage tolerances and decides on stage exceptions, not work package ones.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and represents the supplier view; work package control is the PM's.
whyNot.3: Project support assists with plans and registers; it does not instruct corrective action.

explain.body: Quality tolerance comes from the prioritized acceptance criteria in the project product description and the quality specifications in product descriptions.

test.q: Where does quality tolerance for products come from?
options: The work package description's time and cost targets
The risk register's probability and impact scores
The highlight report's forecast for the stage
test.why: Quality tolerance comes from the prioritized acceptance criteria and the quality specifications for products (8.2.1.2).

whyNot.0: WPD targets and tolerances cover scope, cost and time, not quality.
whyNot.1: Risk scores describe risks, not quality tolerance.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports describe stage status; they do not set tolerance.

explain.body: If one constraint dominates, such as a fixed launch date, it gets the tightest tolerance and others are given more room. Knowing this guides the approach and the tolerances set.

test.q: A product must be ready for a fixed public event. How is this most likely to affect the tolerances set?
options: A tight time tolerance, more room on cost or scope
A wide time tolerance, with tight cost tolerance
Equal tolerances for every aspect of performance
A tight quality tolerance, with more room on time
test.why: When time takes precedence, its tolerance is tight and other constraints are given more room (7.2.4).

whyNot.1: A fixed event makes time the dominant constraint, so its tolerance should be tight, not wide.
whyNot.2: Equal tolerances ignore which constraint takes precedence.
whyNot.3: The fixed event makes time the constraint that takes precedence, so giving time more room is the opposite of what is needed.
